expectations_used.clarify: Pins down, from the visible cases in tests/cases_part1.json through cases_part3.json, that Part 1 guarantees exactly one valid tote pair with no self-pairing, that Part 2 caps at one voucher per lane with a separate total-vouchers budget, and that Part 3's relay may start with either truck or drone rather than a fixed carrier — instead of assuming an unstated variant of any of these.
expectations_used.approach: Names a mechanism per part before typing it: a single-pass hash map from tote weight to position for Part 1; a Dijkstra-style search whose state is (hub, vouchers spent so far) rather than hub alone for Part 2; and a layered BFS tracking (depot, next-required-carrier) rather than a single-color BFS for Part 3.
expectations_used.communicate: States which of the three files is being worked and which mechanism is being encoded as it is typed - e.g. saying that Part 2's state space needs the vouchers-spent dimension because a lane's cost depends on whether a voucher was already spent on it, and that Part 3 needs two BFS frontiers, one per next-expected-carrier - rather than going quiet through the implementation and only speaking again at submit.
expectations_used.implement: Implements solve(tote_weights, pallet_limit) without ever pairing a position with itself, solve(hub_count, lanes, vouchers) so no lane is discounted twice and the search bounds the vouchers-used dimension by vouchers, and solve(depot_count, truck_legs, drone_legs) so entry 0 of the returned array is always 0 and unreachable depots read -1.
expectations_used.verify: Before the one-shot submit, hand-traces all three solutions against their worked examples plus at least one large case from each part's cases file (e.g. the 1000-hub, 25-voucher case in Part 2, or the 15-depot alternating-cycle case in Part 3) rather than trusting the small examples alone to catch a state-space or off-by-one error at the constraint ceiling.
expectations_used.reflect: States, per part, which mechanism was used and what would break it - for example that Part 2's extra state dimension is what keeps a cheaper-but-more-discounted path from being missed, and that Part 3's alternating constraint can make a depot's answer strictly larger than its plain-BFS distance - rather than a one-line 'it passed' summary.

summary: The candidate worked largely in silence through the bulk of the 7-minute session, editing solution_part3.py and solution_part2.py with no real-time narration, then delivered three dense, well-structured speech blocks at the very end covering assumptions, mechanisms, verification, and reflection just before submitting. The final one-shot submission passed all 36 tests, and the closing narration shows correct understanding of all three mechanisms, but the lack of live communication during implementation makes it hard to credit the early stages as genuinely self-directed rather than reconstructed after the fact.

dimensions.analysis: At +404s the candidate explicitly lists the assumptions pulled from the cases files for all three parts (exactly one valid pair with no self-pairing, one voucher per lane with a separate budget, either-carrier start for Part 3), matching exactly the ambiguity the problem calls out. However this articulation happens after most of the implementation was already done (edits to part3 start at +119s, part2 at +371s), so it reads more as a summary of assumptions already baked in rather than upfront resolution before committing to code.

The candidate names the correct mechanisms per part at +404s - single-pass hash map for Part 1, Dijkstra over (hub, vouchers_spent) for Part 2, layered BFS over (depot, carrier_used_to_arrive) for Part 3 - which is exactly the bar the rubric sets. But this statement arrives very late, after most of the coding (the part3 edits stretch from +119s to +331s with no prior narration of the mechanism), so the plan is being recounted post-hoc, not stated as a genuine pre-commitment.

There is a long silent implementation stretch from +119s through +376s covering all the edits to part3 and part2 with zero narration of what mechanism was being encoded or why, followed by three dense speech blocks only at the very end (+404s, +411s, +420s) that retroactively explain the whole session. An interviewer watching live would have had almost nothing to follow during the actual coding.

The many edit/save cycles on solution_part3.py (13 saves between +119s and +331s) suggest iterative refinement of the layered BFS, and the final submission passed all 36 tests, indicating the implementation matched the stated mechanisms competently. However the process itself is opaque - repeated tight edit-save loops on the same file without narration make it hard to distinguish deliberate refinement from trial-and-error thrashing.

At +411s the candidate describes hand-tracing all three solutions against the worked examples plus additional large/edge cases (the 15-depot alternating cycle, the 2-depot self-leg case, disconnected 4-hub case) before the one-shot submit, explicitly naming the risks being checked (missing state dimension in Part 2, single-frontier BFS bug in Part 3). This matches the rubric's bar closely and the final submission going 36/36 confirms the verification was effective.

At +420s the candidate ties each part's outcome back to its mechanism - explaining why the hash map avoids self-pairing, why the extra vouchers_spent dimension prevents double-discounting, and why seeding both carriers at depot 0 makes entry 0 always 0 while same-carrier-only depots stay -1. This goes beyond 'it passed' and shows understanding of why each mechanism was necessary and what would break without it.
